This molecule displays an exceptional tetraradical character ( y 0 = 1.00, y 1 = 0.89) and exhibits long ambient stability ( t 1/2 = 33 days). Comprehensive electronic structure and magnetic response analyses reveal that the spin topology is governed by both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, with robust electron correlation ( J 1 = +321 K, J 2 = −44 K, and J 3 = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness—key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.

articles.title: A single–amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking
articles.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

articles.title: A transcriptional and cellular exploration of obesity and type II diabetes in human adipose tissues
articles.abstract: Obesity is tightly linked to metabolic disorders such as type II diabetes mellitus (T2D), although a subpopulation of individuals with obesity do not present with these morbidities. The biological factors conferring T2D vulnerability remain incompletely understood. We recruited 58 individuals with obesity with or without a clinical diagnosis of T2D (Ob + T2D and Ob). We profiled paired samples of omental and subcutaneous adipose by single-cell RNA sequencing ( n = 10), flow cytometry under basal and stimulated conditions ( n = 42), and histology ( n = 17). Flow cytometry and chemokine quantification were also performed in paired whole blood. We identified reprogramming of the omental stromal compartment, centered on mesothelial and endothelial cells, alongside contrasting innate T cell and macrophage phenotypes across depots. Mesothelial and IGFBP2 + cells exhibited a fibrotic, epithelial-mesenchymal transition–like phenotype, while omental endothelial cells exhibited a lipid-overload, inflammatory, antigen presentation profile in T2D. Omental and subcutaneous adipose innate T cells exhibited divergent inflammatory profiles between tissues. These findings reveal previously unidentified insights into the pathophysiology of T2D in adipose tissue and identify compensatory networks within the tissues that could be exploited by targeted therapeutics.

articles.title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
articles.abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated “locomotion-perception-action” workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.

articles.title: Age reshapes selection on melanoma driver mutations
articles.abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for melanoma. However, it is unclear whether aging fuels tumor evolution by altering mutation rates, changing the microenvironmentally induced selection on drivers, or both. We analyzed 5472 melanomas, estimating how selection on individual variants changes with patient age while accounting for differing neutral mutation rates. Neutral mutation rates increased only modestly with age; ultraviolet damage remained predominant, but endogenous processes increasingly contributed to older tumors. In contrast, selection on major drivers was strongly age dependent: The advantage of BRAF V600E declined precipitously with age, whereas NRAS Q61 mutations gained advantage. TERT promoter mutations became more frequent, yet less advantageous. Aging therefore reshapes melanoma evolution primarily by altering selection, motivating age-conscious evaluation of clinical biomarkers and therapies.

articles.title: Brainstem enkephalinergic neural circuit underlying cold-induced pain relief in mice
articles.abstract: Application of cold or cold-mimicking chemicals to injury has long been recognized as an effective means of pain relief. However, underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified a cold-responsive neuronal subset within the lateral parabrachial nucleus (lPBN), the thermosensory relay region in the hindbrain, that mediates cold-induced analgesia in mice. Activation of these neurons and their projection to ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) increased the nociceptive threshold, while ablation of these neurons attenuated analgesia induced by cold-mimicking chemicals. We further identified that these neurons express precursor gene of enkephalin ( Penk ), which is necessary for TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8)–mediated pain relief. Mechanistically, cold-responsive lPBN neurons frequency-dependently released enkephalin peptide into vlPAG to activate the descending pain modulation circuitry via disinhibition. Activation of cold-responsive neurons reduced spinal cord responses to noxious stimuli, suggesting the involvement of a top-down pain modulation pathway. These findings propose a central mechanism underlying cold-induced pain relief, which could be a novel therapeutic target.

articles.title: CD8+ T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
articles.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)–regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell–dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell–mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell–induced endothelial death in CM.

articles.title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii: Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
articles.abstract: Aeromonas , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance in Aeromonas strains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol’s antibacterial mechanisms against Aeromonas veronii and evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5′-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against A. veronii , with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

articles.title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
articles.abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

articles.title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
articles.abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.

articles.title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
articles.abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

articles.title: Erratum for the Research Article “A combinational chemo-immune therapy using an enzyme-sensitive nanoplatform for dual-drug delivery to specific sites by cascade targeting”
Erratum for the Research Article “CD38-mediated metabolic reprogramming promotes the stability and suppressive function of regulatory T cells in tumor”
Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
articles.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

articles.title: High-impulse and reactant-regenerative combustion-based micro actuators
articles.abstract: The use of combustibles in micro-actuator technologies enables powerful impulsive actuation capabilities comparable to those of natural organisms. However, the exogenous dependence of fuel limits the development of combustion-based actuators. We present a closed-cycle reactant regeneration strategy wherein the bidirectional interconversion between hydrogen and water achieves real-time fuel replenishment for reactant-regenerative electrolysis and combustion reactions. Based on this, we develop a 1.5-centimeter actuator that generates forces above 20 newtons and operates continuously for >7200 cycles without refueling (a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over existing combustion-based actuators). Experiments confirm its strength and cross-environment versatility for removing obstacles, jetting, and striking via underwater cavitation. These features enable the actuator to be integrated into small robotic platforms, allowing them to reconfigure local surroundings in an active manner.

articles.title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
articles.abstract: The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

articles.title: Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
articles.abstract: Many terrestrial insects transition from humid to dry environments at metamorphosis, yet how they avoid dehydration is unclear. In Drosophila melanogaster , we identify a lipid barrier to water loss in the pupa that is anatomically distinct from that of the adult. It comprises unisex hydrocarbons that are longer and less volatile than their sex-specific adult counterparts. These hyperlong hydrocarbons are produced by larval oenocytes and stored in the fat body for subsequent transport to the cuticle at pupariation. A fatty acid elongase, EloHL, is required for hyperlong hydrocarbon biosynthesis and for a functional barrier to dehydration during early metamorphosis. Hyperlong barrier hydrocarbons are widespread across the Drosophila genus and typically transition to shorter sex-specific versions during adult maturation. In the desert species D. mojavensis , however, adults retain hyperlong hydrocarbons. This study reveals how insect lipid barriers are tuned to environmental variations in aridity and temperature during development and evolution.

articles.title: MYC primes a paralog synthetic lethality involving the mitochondrial translocase subunits TIMM17A and TIMM17B and N-Acetylaspartate
articles.abstract: To identify the genes and pathways required for the survival of MYC -amplified cancers, we engineered an isogenic cell system in which transformation is driven by oncogenic MYC . Using a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 library, we identified the mitochondrial membrane translocase TIMM17A as uniquely essential for the survival of MYC-transformed cells. This dependency arises from MYC-driven suppression of TIMM17B , the paralog of TIMM17A . TIMM17A/B is an essential component of the TIM23 mitochondrial protein import complex, and the MYC-induced suppression of TIMM17B creates a strong dependency on TIMM17A . N-acetylaspartate supplementation rescued TIMM17A dependency in MYC -amplified cell lines, highlighting the unique and crucial role of this metabolite in the cell fitness of MYC -amplified cancers. These observations identify a paralog dependency required for the survival of a subset of MYC-driven cancers.

articles.title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
articles.abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.

articles.title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
articles.abstract: Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Double-negative regulatory T cells (DNTreg) are important immune regulatory cells that maintain liver immune homeostasis. However, their survival and function are compromised in MASLD. Herein, we found that mevalonate pathway and its rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) were significantly down-regulated in DNTreg from both mice and patients with MASLD, correlating with impaired DNTreg viability and immunosuppressive function. Arachidonic acid is enriched in MASLD liver and inhibits DNTreg HMGCR expression. Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), a downstream product of HMGCR, mediates RAC1 geranylgeranylation, which facilitates its interaction with mitochondrial CLPX protease, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and immunoregulatory activity of DNTreg. Adoptive transfer of Pggt1b +/− DNTreg into MASLD mice demonstrated significantly diminished therapeutic efficacy compared with wild-type DNTreg. In conclusion, mevalonate metabolism–mediated geranylgeranylation is essential for the suppressive activity and immune homeostasis of DNTreg in MASLD.

articles.title: Molecular engineering of noncoordinating backbones in Zr-MOFs for ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism-based high pressure sensing
articles.abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising pressure-responsive luminescent materials, but precise control of their emission under pressure remains a substantial challenge. Here, we engineered the piezofluorochromic response of zirconium-based MOFs by tuning the polarity of the emissive moieties through noncoordinating phenyl substituents. Four isostructural UiO-67 derivatives were synthesized. The most polar ligand, in UiO-67-PA, yields ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism with a bathochromic shift of 190 nanometers per gigapascal below 0.36 gigapascals. This sensitivity arises from two cooperative effects: enhanced conjugation through pressure-driven rotation of the aromatic rings and amplified orbital overlap resulting from polarity-induced electronic redistribution. This work broadens the strategies for modulating MOF luminescence and highlights their potential for pressure sensing.

articles.title: Photonic entanglement swapping with remote quantum dots
articles.abstract: Entanglement swapping is a protocol that details how to create entanglement between previously uncorrelated particles. Its photonic version, mediated by the interference of photon pairs generated by separate quantum systems, finds disparate applications in quantum networks. So far, entanglement swapping with entangled photons from remote systems has been implemented only using probabilistic sources. However, the scaling up of quantum networks requires nonprobabilistic quantum emitters without a trade-off between the degree of entanglement and photon-pair generation rate. Here, we demonstrate photonic entanglement swapping using photon pairs generated by two separate GaAs quantum dots. The emitters are deterministically embedded in hybrid semiconductor-piezoelectric devices that make the entangled photons from two dissimilar quantum dots nearly identical. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated with a fidelity as high as 0.71(2), more than 10 SDs above the classical limit. The experimental data are quantitatively explained by a theoretical model that also suggests how to boost the protocol performance. Our work opens the path to the exploitation of quantum dot entangled-photon sources in quantum repeater networks.

articles.title: Pink noise in dyads’ semantic similarity trajectories predicts conversation enjoyment
articles.abstract: Conversation is a core component of human social life. Many influential theories treat conversation as a linear system, i.e., the sum of its parts. However, linear accounts of semantic entrainment lose explanatory power at their upper limits: Discussing perfectly aligned opinions becomes boring. We propose an alternate account that considers the multiscale organization of semantic similarity over the course of a conversation, as indexed by pink noise. Here, we test whether pink noise can be found in interlocutors’ conavigated trajectories through semantic space. Not only is pink noise present, but its strength predicts positive conversation outcomes like enjoyment and connection, increases with practice, and is reflected in a large language model’s representation of conversation quality. These results demonstrate an important role for scale-free dynamics in characterizing successful conversation.

articles.title: Prebiotic magnetite enables chirality-magnetic surface feedback
articles.abstract: The emergence of biomolecular homochirality requires both an initial symmetry-breaking event and a mechanism to amplify and preserve a chiral imbalance. Magnetic minerals have been shown to function as chiral agents through the chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect and may have enabled homochirality on early Earth, yet the magnetic properties of magnetite formed under realistic prebiotic conditions remain unexplored. Here, we show that magnetite synthesized through two geochemically plausible pathways—UV-driven photo-oxidation and nitrite-mediated oxidation of Fe(II)—produces particles dominated by single-vortex and multivortex magnetic domain states. Magnetic measurements and electron microscopy confirm that these populations differ markedly from the nano-fabricated thin-film substrates conventionally used in previous CISS experiments. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that single-domain and vortex-state grains undergo irreversible, exchange-driven remagnetization when interacting with spin-polarized homochiral compounds. This magnetic irreversibility provides a robust mechanism for storing and reinforcing weak chiral bias, suggesting that prebiotic magnetite could have contributed to the emergence and stabilization of persistent chiral bias on early Earth.

articles.title: Quantum-interference metrology of dissipative Kerr solitons
articles.abstract: Dissipative Kerr solitons in optical microresonators underpin chip-scale frequency combs with applications ranging from coherent telecommunications to precision spectroscopy. Yet the characterization of their intrinsic femtosecond temporal structure remains challenging, as the low pulse energy and broad spectral bandwidth necessitate optical amplification and careful dispersion compensation in conventional ultrafast diagnostics, both of which can substantial distort the waveform. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-interference metrology of microcomb solitons based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By attenuating the soliton stream to the single-photon level and measuring fourth-order interference, we directly retrieve near transform-limited pulse durations without amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate even after propagation through 25 kilometers of standard fiber. The same interferogram also provides direct access to the temporal separations in multisoliton states by converting intersoliton separations into additional interference dips at corresponding delays, enabling subpicosecond characterization of their intracavity temporal structure. This quantum-inspired paradigm introduces a metrological approach that is immune to amplification and dispersion distortions, offering a powerful tool for the characterization of complex soliton physics.

articles.title: Reciprocal control of genome instability and RNA processing in cancer: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities
articles.abstract: Genomic instability and dysregulated RNA processing are each recognized as core hallmarks of cancer, but accumulating evidence indicates that they are mechanistically intertwined rather than independent features. Chromosomal instability, mismatch-repair deficiency, and homologous recombination deficiency can reshape RNA splicing, 3′ end formation, and RNA surveillance through changes in gene dosage, DNA damage signaling, and alterations in regulatory elements. Conversely, aberrant splicing, polyadenylation, and RNA modifications can impair DNA repair, perturb mitotic control, and promote replication stress, thereby reinforcing genomic instability. This bidirectional circuit drives clinically relevant phenotypes, including therapeutic resistance, immune modulation, and emergent vulnerabilities that are not captured by DNA-centric biomarkers alone. Here, we present a unified framework for the genome instability–RNA processing axis and its direct clinical implications for cancer diagnosis, treatment stratification, and therapeutic exploitation, highlighting the most actionable mechanistic interfaces and discussing how integrated DNA-RNA biomarkers and rational combination strategies could extend precision oncology beyond static genomic lesions.

articles.title: Revisiting the additionality and durability of carbon uptake in large-scale ocean iron fertilization
articles.abstract: Climate stabilization pathways limiting global warming to 1.5° to 2°C require rapid emission reductions alongside additional carbon dioxide removal (CDR) of ∼2 to 3 PgC year −1 . Our simulations show that sustained century-scale ocean iron fertilization (OIF) in the southern sector of the Southern Ocean (SSO) provides a contribution of ∼30 PgC, equivalent to ∼0.3 PgC year −1 . This uptake nearly matches the additional carbon uptake from global fertilization. In other iron-limited regions, fertilization-induced uptake is largely offset (70 to 100%) by anomalous outgassing in nonfertilized regions. After terminating OIF following 30 years of fertilization, the ocean retains ∼50% of the additional carbon in the SSO, whereas retention is negligible elsewhere. These results identify the SSO as the most favorable region for durable carbon removal through large-scale OIF, particularly in terms of additionality and durability, although its carbon uptake is smaller than earlier estimates. OIF-induced CDR is constrained by local and remote nutrient depletion, carbon reentrainment, incomplete macronutrient drawdown, and reduced phytoplankton carbon-to-phosphorus ratios. Incomplete macronutrient drawdown reflects the uptake controls by light, top-down controls, and rates of macronutrient resupply. Further insight into OIF potential will be enabled by standardized multimodel comparisons and targeted analysis of nutrient drawdown controls.

articles.title: Scaling up chemical recycling: High-yield polyolefin pyrolysis to liquid hydrocarbons using iron single atom catalysts
articles.abstract: The chemical recycling of polyolefins (PO) via pyrolysis offers a circular pathway for plastic waste management, yet industrial implementation remains hindered by high energy demands and poor product selectivity. Here, we report an Fe-catalyzed pyrolysis process that achieves 97% PO conversion and a 94% yield of C6 to C35 liquid hydrocarbons. By using a zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF)–derived, N-doped porous carbon-supported iron single-atom catalyst (Fe 1 @NC) in combination with a strategic temperature gradient control, we overcome traditional thermolysis limitations. The process was further demonstrated on a kilogram scale, supporting the practical scalability of this catalytic system. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the rate-determining step is an acid base–promoted dehydrogenation of the polymer backbone. Specifically, electronic synergy between the single iron centers and the carbon support stabilizes reactive carbocation intermediates, facilitating their rapid decomposition into high-value olefins and alkanes. These findings provide a scalable and highly efficient catalytic framework for the upcycling of plastic waste into liquid hydrocarbon fractions and chemical feedstocks.

articles.title: Shape-memory scaffold targets inflammation and fibrosis to restore endometrium and fertility in intrauterine adhesions
articles.abstract: Intrauterine adhesion (IUA) is a major cause of infertility, yet current treatments remain limited in preventing fibrosis and restoring functional endometrium. We report a bi-drug, bifunctional, biodegradable shape-memory regenerative (BiSMR) scaffold enabling minimally invasive implantation, sequential drug release, and barrier protection. Proteomic profiling of chemical, mechanical, and combined injury models revealed inflammatory activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired regenerative programs, providing a molecular rationale for combining epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) with 17β-estradiol (E 2 ). BiSMR couples an E 2 -loaded PLTG [poly( l -lactide)- co -trimethylene carbonate- co -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E 2 delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.

articles.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux
articles.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

articles.title: Spatial proteomics reveals lipid droplet reorganization in symbiotic Paramecium bursaria cells
articles.abstract: Endosymbiosis is an important adaptive mechanism allowing organisms to exploit previously inaccessible niches. The flexible relationship between the ciliate Paramecium bursaria and green algae represents a model system for studying early endosymbiosis evolution. However, the mechanisms underlying how P. bursaria cells maintain this endosymbiotic relationship remain unclear. Here, we use mass spectrometry–based proteomics to generate a spatial proteomic atlas of the host P. bursaria cells with and without endosymbionts. This atlas defines the protein composition of the endosymbiont-containing compartment (perialgal vacuole) and reveals pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets upon symbiosis. Imaging analyses confirm that lipid droplets change in size, morphology, and positioning, accumulating near intracellular algae. Perturbing symbiotic cells with chemical inhibitors of lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiotic algal numbers, revealing a role for lipid droplets in the host-endosymbiont interaction. Our data provide a comprehensive resource for protein localization in P. bursaria cells and elucidate how those cells remodel an existing cellular compartment to maintain endosymbiosis.

articles.title: Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
articles.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.

articles.title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery
articles.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo–electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli –infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

articles.title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
articles.abstract: Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, with CD4 + cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.

articles.title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD+ precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal
articles.abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD + via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila , along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.

articles.title: Three-way circulation–soil moisture–temperature feedbacks amplify the most extreme mid-latitudinal heat waves
articles.abstract: The most extreme heat waves are intensifying faster than moderate events across many mid-latitude regions. Climate models underestimate these trends, suggesting an incomplete representation and understanding of the underlying physical processes. Here, we use an explainable machine-learning framework to investigate interactions among atmospheric circulation, surface soil moisture, and temperature, and their role in recent heat extremes. We show that a three-way interaction among these components becomes active once a critical temperature threshold is exceeded, contributing, on average, ∼10% to peak temperature anomalies during the most extreme heat events across ∼28% of humid mid-latitude regions. We further reveal that this interaction is systematically underestimated in CMIP6 and CESM2 Large Ensemble simulations. Soils in climate models are too dry at the initiation of heat waves, therefore suppressing subsequent soil-moisture depletion and inhibiting feedback activation. These findings help explain regional model biases in upper-tail warming and highlight avenues for improving future projections of extreme heat events.

articles.title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
articles.abstract: Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10 −7 hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.

articles.title: Visualizing nanoscopic acoustic mode competition in a van der Waals ferroelectric
articles.abstract: Understanding how low-dimensional ferroelectrics respond to ultrafast excitation at nanoscales is essential for controlling energy flow and mechanical functionality in next-generation polar devices, yet the nanoscopic structural response to ultrafast depolarization remains unresolved, obscuring the microscopic pathways of acoustic decoherence and energy dissipation. Here, we spatiotemporally resolve lattice motion in the van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI 2 using combined ultrafast electron microscopy and diffraction, revealing three acoustic phonons: two transverse shear modes and one longitudinal breathing mode. The transverse mode that shears the layers perpendicular to the in-plane polar axis dominates over that along the polar axis, reflecting anisotropic polarization-strain coupling. Real-space mapping uncovers spatially correlated heterogeneity in mode amplitudes and lifetimes. Regions dominated by a single shear mode exhibit significantly longer acoustic lifetimes than multimode regions, suggesting acoustic phonon–phonon scattering as a major source of decoherence. Our results provide a microscopic understanding of ultrafast depolarization-driven acoustic dynamics and spatially heterogeneous energy dissipation in van der Waals ferroelectrics.

articles.title: Y chromosome instability in the early mouse embryo
articles.abstract: The Y chromosome lacks canonical centromeric repeats necessary for high-fidelity chromosome segregation. In adult tissues, this causes Y loss and predisposes to disease. However, its impact on embryogenesis is unknown. Here, we identify the first mouse embryonic mitoses as a window during which the Y centromere is unusually weak. This vulnerability impairs kinetochore strength and the Y becomes preferentially trapped at the spindle pole, resulting in missegregation. To study the impact of Y loss, we generate an aggregation model to track specific aneuploidies in mosaic embryos. Loss of the Y slows down cell division and compromises embryo size. Our findings reveal a developmental window during which the Y is especially vulnerable to loss, with implications for male sex determination and the origin of Turner syndrome (XO).

articles.title: Collateral damage…or is love really blind?
articles.abstract: Bystander T cells eradicate tumors in the absence of antigen recognition.

articles.title: Myeloid cells run amok in injured brains
articles.abstract: Aberrant, cranial bone marrow–derived myelopoiesis drives neuroinflammation in chronic traumatic brain injury.

articles.title: Programming immunity in situ: A new frontier of in vivo cell engineering
articles.abstract: In vivo cell engineering enables the direct programming of immune cells inside patients. Instead of isolating, modifying, and reinfusing cells, therapeutic instructions are delivered directly to selected immune cells through lipid nanoparticles or viral vectors. This approach could facilitate rapid and scalable deployment of varied immune cell therapies across disease contexts. Early clinical studies in oncology and autoimmunity demonstrate increasing technical and clinical feasibility. The next challenge lies in enhancing precision to ensure that vectors reach the target cell type and tissue, deliver the appropriate payload, and produce desired transient or durable activity. Progress in targeting ligands, vector design, biodistribution control, and genome editing is beginning to address these barriers. Ensuring safety against immunogenicity, inflammatory toxicity, off-target editing, and uncontrolled persistence remains a central priority. By mastering these constraints, in vivo engineering could turn endogenous immune cells into therapeutic agents generated directly in the body, expanding cell therapy to diseases refractory to current modalities.

articles.title: The structural basis of IL-36R proinflammatory signaling mediated by IL-36γ and IL-37
articles.abstract: The interleukin-36 receptor (IL-36R) drives proinflammatory signaling and is therapeutically targeted by spesolimab in acute skin inflammation. Beyond its three canonical agonists (IL-36α, IL-36β, and IL-36γ), IL-36R was recently proposed to be activated by IL-37. Together with antagonism by IL-36R antagonist (IL-36RA) and IL-38, this creates a complex structure-function landscape that remains poorly understood. Here, we report the cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of human IL-36γ bound to IL-36R and the shared co-receptor IL-1R accessory protein (IL-1RAcP). IL-36γ engages IL-36R with low affinity, enabling high-affinity IL-1RAcP recruitment. IL-37 exhibits the opposite binding signature, binding IL-36R with high affinity but IL-1RAcP weakly. Functional comparison of IL-36R engagement by IL-36γ and IL-37 confirmed their common proinflammatory signature, with IL-36γ exhibiting markedly higher potency, consistent with its more stable signaling complex. Structural comparison of cytokine-bound versus antibody-antagonized IL-36R revealed that spesolimab acts as an allosteric antagonist. This study therefore provides a structural and mechanistic blueprint for IL-36R activation by distinct cytokines.

articles.title: A simplified high-pressure freezing workflow in Autogrids
articles.abstract: Weber et al. introduce a modular planchette system that simplifies high-pressure freezing of biological samples for cryo-electron microscopy. By reducing sample handling and accommodating diverse specimen types, the Autogrid planchette approach makes it easier to study complex biological structures in their near-native state, expanding opportunities for cellular and biomedical research.

articles.title: Covalent remodeling of CRBN creates a non-canonical neosubstrate interface with NTAQ1
articles.abstract: De la Peña, Cruite et al. show that covalent modification of cereblon (CRBN) creates a new neosubstrate-binding interface that recruits NTAQ1 through a mechanism distinct from canonical G-loop degrons. This work reveals how site-specific chemical modification can reprogram E3 ligase specificity and expand the design space for molecular glue degraders.

articles.title: Dynamic ring rearrangements underlie transport by MCE proteins
articles.abstract: Ratkevičiūtė et al. identify inter-ring conformational plasticity as a shared property of structurally distinct MCE proteins. Coordinated ring and pore rearrangements dynamically reshape the central transport channel, providing a structural basis for substrate translocation and revealing how mutations triggering channel collapse can disrupt MCE protein function.

articles.title: Doctor who faked CV to secure NHS hospital job is struck off
articles.abstract: A doctor who made 20 false claims in his CV to secure an NHS job that he was not qualified for has been struck off the UK medical register.1Tochukwu Akah, who qualified as a doctor in Nigeria in 2016, was appointed as a clinical fellow in haematology at Hampshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust in September 2024.A medical practitioners tribunal heard that Akah admitted falsely claiming to have completed several courses, attained wide experience, authored a journal article, and received awards.Akah claimed that he had been a chief medical officer in an emergency department in Nigeria, had published a research article on sickle cell disease, and had independently completed tens of thousands of intravenous cannulation procedures, venous blood sampling procedures, and blood transfusions.Akah also falsely claimed to have won the “best student in internal medicine” and “distinction in pathology” awards at university and to have independent practical experience in exchange blood...

articles.title: French blood service is targeted in wave of refrigeration cyberattacks across Europe
articles.abstract: France’s national blood service said one of its refrigeration monitoring and control suppliers was hacked on Monday, raising temperature and defrost thresholds in cold rooms at three preparation or distribution sites to “very high levels.”The attack came as more than 10 European countries, including France and the UK, were hit by cyberattacks1 at supermarket chains that also remotely manipulated refrigeration thermostats, turning them up to 50°C (122°F) or forcing defrost modes and spoiling large amounts of fresh food. Investigators have yet to establish whether the attacks were linked.Unlike the supermarkets, which had to jettison massive quantities of overheated fresh and frozen food, the blood stocks came out unscathed, the blood service Établissement français du sang (EFS) said.An EFS spokesperson told The BMJ that the cold rooms normally operated at -30°C but would not confirm a report in the French newspaper Le Canard enchaîné that hackers had reprogrammed the equipment to...

articles.title: Lab leak disease outbreaks: the long, murky history
articles.abstract: In the heart of Russia, fear of plague is spreading. Unbeknown to the outside world, authorities have quietly commandeered the building where the first case emerged. Rifle wielding guards stand at the entrances. Inside, people are locked in quarantine rooms. There have already been deaths—pneumonic plague. And it came from a laboratory.This was the scene at a Moscow hospital in 1939, according to a handful of recollections written by scientists who lived through it. The microbiologist Abram Lvovich Berlin had travelled in from the outskirts of the capital to discuss his experiments with Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague. But he had inadvertently infected himself, becoming highly contagious. He would soon be dead.Sources differ on the details—was it two or three people who succumbed after coming into contact with Berlin? Most accounts say that the doctor who first diagnosed plague in the stricken microbiologist and a hotel barber were...

articles.title: Managing risk and uncertainty includes ambiguity
articles.abstract: jason.hancock@nhs.netChris Whitty’s recent lecture on risk, uncertainty, and medical decision making resonated with my experience as a psychiatrist, director of medical education, and clinical education researcher with an interest in uncertainty.1 I welcome his suggestion that educators should support resident doctors to hold and manage progressively greater levels of risk throughout their training.But the lecture placed considerable emphasis on probability and complexity as sources of uncertainty, with less attention given to ambiguity.2 Whitty called for the medical profession to insist that large language models used by the public indicate the degree of uncertainty associated with a proposed diagnosis, for example. This assumes that the level of uncertainty can be quantified, as may be possible when uncertainty arises from probability. But many clinical decisions are made in the context of ambiguity—where information is missing, imprecise, or conflicting—and the degree of uncertainty may not be known or straightforward to communicate.The skills needed...

articles.title: Palantir’s NHS contract: Government prepares to put deal out to open tender
articles.abstract: The government is planning to put its NHS contract with the controversial US tech giant Palantir out to competitive tender, The BMJ understands.The move to retender the Federated Data Platform (FDP) contract would force Palantir to rebid against UK based competitors.A source at one British company with similar technology to the US giant, who wished to remain anonymous, told The BMJ that officials at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) had approached a handful of British companies to see whether they had the capacity to run the FDP.The BMJ understands that the government will extend the deal by two years to minimise disruption while the retendering process occurs.The move comes as the Financial Times reported that the UK government was preparing to extend Palantir’s contract next year while ministers draw up plans to potentially replace it with a British alternative.1The £182m FDP has a break clause in February...

articles.title: Science Media Centre “legitimises” industries that harm health, study claims
articles.abstract: A science communication organisation that provides expertise to major UK media outlets “amplifies” and “legitimises” the stances of “health harming industries,” new research concludes.1The Science Media Centre (SMC), which is based at the London headquarters of its major backer, Wellcome, provides interviews and press briefings on breaking science news to journalists at leading outlets across the UK. Its clients include The BMJ.But a study by researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) and the University of Edinburgh finds that the centre’s funding model “legitimises health harming industries as partners in public health endeavours.”SMC’s chief executive, Fiona Fox, defended the model, arguing that accepting small “no strings attached” donations from large numbers of organisations protected its editorial independence from individual corporate agendas.Researchers analysed SMC funding and governance data and extracted “SMC Rapid Reactions” on research studies from 2019, chosen because this was a pre-pandemic year in which...

articles.title: [Clinical Rounds] Vertigo, multifocal brain lesions, and a diagnostic clue on the skin
articles.abstract: A woman aged 35 years was evaluated for a 1-year history of recurrent, brief (approximately 15 min) episodes of non-positional vertigo described as a spinning sensation. Episodes were not accompanied by headache, tinnitus, hearing loss, visual symptoms, or other neurological complaints. Blood pressure was normal, and there was no orthostatic hypotension or tachycardia upon standing. Neurological and vestibular examinations, including audiometry and the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre, were normal between episodes.

articles.title: [Comment] Preparing for dialysis when dialysis might never begin?
articles.abstract: For older people (aged ≥80 years) with frailty or multimorbidity living with kidney failure, choosing a care pathway could involve deciding whether to prepare for dialysis long before it is needed. Preparation involves education, appointments, investigations, and, for some people, surgery to create dialysis access. The alternative care pathway is conservative kidney management, which involves active care aimed at slowing kidney disease progression, managing symptoms, and preserving quality of life without planning for dialysis.

articles.title: Mastering the role of radiotherapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: who and why?
Catalytic domains encode product diversity in PUFA synthases
articles.abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) synthases share similar architectures, yet produce distinct PUFAs. Recent mechanistic studies reveal how substrate recognition by dehydratase, ketoacyl-acyl carrier protein synthase, and acyltransferase domains controls double bond formation, chain elongation, and release, highlighting chemical principles underlying PUFA structural diversity and product distributions. These insights inform rational engineering.

articles.title: Inner-sphere iron photocatalysis unlocks direct decarboxylative borylation
articles.abstract: Carboxylic acids are attractive precursors to boronic esters, but redox requirements of decarboxylation are poorly matched to diboron reagents. Juliá-Hernández and coworkers report an iron ligand-to-metal charge transfer strategy activating coordinated carboxylates through photoinduced electron transfer. Free acids, from acetic acid to drug molecules, give boronic esters in one step.

articles.title: Strategic innovation in the total synthesis of Euphorbia diterpenoids
articles.abstract: Following Wender’s pioneering studies, the total synthesis of Euphorbia diterpenoids has undergone a remarkable renaissance over the past decade. This resurgence has been driven by the emergence of unified synthetic platforms, radical-based coupling strategies, and strategic cycloaddition reactions. These developments have not only enabled the concise and scalable synthesis of flagship molecules such as phorbol, prostratin, resiniferatoxin, and pedrolide, but also provided chemical probes for exploring their promising biological activities. This review summarizes the total syntheses of these four molecules, with a particular emphasis on the strategic innovations and emerging trends across the different synthetic routes developed for each, aiming to provide timely guidance for future synthetic efforts.

articles.title: A new view of collectivism
articles.abstract: Collectivism is the most widely studied cultural dimension. Yet recent evidence shows that the most-cited scales contain conflicting definitions of collectivism. I review evidence that conceptualizations conflate ‘warm fuzzy’ collectivism and responsibilism. I outline how clarifying the concept can resolve apparent contradictions in previous findings and advance measurement and theory.

articles.title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices
articles.abstract: Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

articles.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
articles.abstract: What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?

articles.title: Embracing ignorance: tackling biodiversity knowledge shortfalls
articles.abstract: Global biodiversity information suffers from gaps, biases, and uncertainty over time and space, afflicting all taxonomic groups. Incomplete or biased data introduce uncertainty into models of biodiversity trends, potentially generating faulty inferences with knock-on effects for conservation. We revisit how the limitations of biodiversity knowledge are conceptualised, expanding the current classification to encompass eleven major shortfalls spanning taxonomic, ecological, evolutionary, and biocultural aspects, and examine the impediments that limit progress in reducing them. Information gaps have been moulded by our capacity and willingness to collect data, which are constrained by a series of financial, taxonomic, and technological impediments that vary across regions and taxa. Addressing these challenges is crucial for understanding biodiversity patterns and processes and developing effective conservation actions.

articles.title: A novel KIR3DL2-directed CAR T-cell therapy for cutaneous and systemic T-cell lymphomas
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but its extension to T-cell lymphomas (TCLs) has been constrained by the paucity of antigens that can be safely targeted. While targeting pan-T antigens broadens the therapeutic reach across various TCLs, it carries a substantial risk of immunosuppression and infection. Here, we report killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, three Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 2 (KIR3DL2/CD158k) as a viable target for CAR T-cell therapy against a wide range of TCLs. Using single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and flow cytometric phenotyping, we observed that KIR3DL2 expression is restricted to a subset of mature NK cells and a minor fraction of CD8⁺ T cells, with negligible expression in other healthy adult tissues. Among TCLs, KIR3DL2 expression was noted in various subtypes of cutaneous and systemic TCLs. Anti-KIR3DL2 CAR constructs (3DL2CARs) efficiently and selectively redirected T cells against antigen-positive cell lines but not isogenic KIR3DL2-negative counterparts, with antigen-specific signaling, cytotoxicity, proliferation, and cytokine production. Importantly, 3DL2CART cells produced sustained tumor regression and prolonged survival in two distinct cell line-derived xenograft models of cutaneous TCL and in one patient-derived xenograft model of hepatosplenic TCL. 3DL2CART cells exhibited minimal off-target activity against bystander immune cells and showed no appreciable fratricide. To mitigate the risk of tumor cell contamination in autologous CAR T-cell products, we established a two-tiered strategy that integrates immunomagnetic depletion of KIR3DL2-positive tumor cells with in vivo activation of a safety switch if inadvertently transduced malignant cells contribute to immune escape. Together, our results establish the preclinical efficacy and safety of 3DL2CART-cell therapy and support its clinical translation. This approach may offer a targeted alternative to pan-T-cell-directed CAR T-cell strategies for patients with relapsed/refractory cutaneous and systemic TCLs, addressing a critical unmet clinical need.

articles.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
articles.abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

articles.title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
articles.abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV-associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.

articles.title: Analysis of reproductive traits associated with lipoprotein(a) deficiency in participants from the Pakistan Genome Resource
articles.abstract: Aims. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, driving development of LPA-targeting therapies that markedly lower circulating Lp(a). Because LPA?the gene encoding apolipoprotein(a)?is absent in most model organisms, preclinical studies have limited value for assessing effects such as reproductive safety. Therefore, naturally occurring human LPA ?knockouts? were analyzed to evaluate reproductive outcomes of on-target Lp(a) lowering. Methods and Results. Individuals carrying high-confidence LPA loss-of-function (LoF) variants which reduce Lp(a) in a gene-dosage?dependent manner within the Pakistan Genome Resource were identified. LoF variants showed no depletion of homozygotes relative to Hardy?Weinberg expectations. LPA LoF associations with fertility-related traits (ever having a child and number of children) under additive and recessive models were assessed using regenie-based burden testing, including sex-stratified analyses, and no significant associations were observed. A recall-by-genotype study of female LoF homozygotes alongside heterozygous and non-carrier family member controls was performed, surveying reproductive histories and offspring outcomes. Across 107 pregnancies and 87 children in 19 homozygous LoF women, rates of miscarriage, maternal complications (including preeclampsia, hypertension, and gestational diabetes), delivery complications, neonatal intensive care admission, birth defects, and child health problems were comparable across genotypes with no statistically significant genotype?outcome associations. Conclusions. These genetic and by-genotype analyses indicate that complete lifelong LPA deficiency due to high-confidence LPA loss-of-function variants is not associated with overt adverse maternal fertility, pregnancy or child health outcomes. These findings offer human genetic reassurance regarding reproductive and developmental safety in the context of sustained Lp(a)-lowering, with implications for long-term therapies targeting Lp(a).

articles.title: Asymmetric division and polar growth define a non-canonical cell cycle in Bradyrhizobium.
articles.abstract: Bradyrhizobia are widely used as plant growth promoters in agriculture, yet their cell biology remains poorly understood. Here, we described for the first time, nucleoid segregation dynamics and the cell cycle of Bradyrhizobium at the cellular level. We show that highly asymmetric polar growth generates a short daughter cell and a longer mother cell at each division. Nucleoid compaction and positioning change across growth phases, culminating in a highly compacted, asymmetrically positioned nucleoid in stationary phase. ParB presents a subpolar localization, at the nucleoid periphery. Despite this pronounced cellular asymmetry and the presence of a single large chromosome, chromosome conformation capture reveals a global chromosome organization similar to that of bacteria undergoing conventional binary fission Together, these findings uncover a distinctive cell cycle program in Bradyrhizobium. showing that such extreme asymmetry in growth and division, significantly different from closely related characterized α-Proteobacteriota, is compatible with conserved principles of chromosome organization.

articles.title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
articles.abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

articles.title: Brief visual oddball events evoke CSF flow in the spinal canal
articles.abstract: The measurement of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow with fMRI, made possible by exploiting edge artifacts of spin saturation when the bottom acquisition slice lies in a CSF reservoir, allows researchers to investigate an aspect of brain health that has been increasingly linked to cognitive aging and neurodegenerative disease via its role in glymphatic clearance. The initial demonstration of this technique used the fourth ventricle, but recent reports show it can also be done when the bottom acquisition slice lies in the spinal canal in the foramen magnum. We present a method to automatically identify the spinal canal without manual tracing, and measure CSF flow with high confidence using multi-echo acquisition to separate out BOLD-like and non-BOLD-like signal components, along with physiological regression to improve signal to noise ratio. Using these methods we found that CSF flow correlated with decreases in BOLD activity in 70 adults aged 19-76. We further found that brief, infrequent salient stimuli (visual oddballs, requiring a button press) were capable of provoking measurable CSF flow.

articles.title: Broad Cognitive and Motivational Enhancement through M4-Selective Muscarinic Modulation
articles.abstract: The muscarinic M4 subtype of acetylcholine receptors is part of agonist compounds considered treatment options for Schizophrenia and Alzheimers disease, but how M4-subtype selective modulation affects cognition and motivation is largely unknown due to dose-limiting side effects, a scarcity of receptor-selective compounds, and missing multi-domain assessments of cognition. Here, we surmount these constraints by utilizing a M4-selective positive allosteric modulator (PAM) to assess in nonhuman primates a broad array of endpoints spanning motivational effort control and multiple executive function domains.
