articles.title: Review of Adult Male Hypogonadism
articles.abstract: To the Editor A recent Review of adult male hypogonadism thoroughly discussed several important treatment-related adverse effects and safety considerations of testosterone use, including erythrocytosis, venous thromboembolic events, blood pressure elevation, and prostate-related monitoring. However, one clinically important adverse effect of testosterone therapy was overlooked: suppression of spermatogenesis and the subsequent risk of infertility in reproductive-aged men.

articles.title: Review of Adult Male Hypogonadism—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We appreciate the letter about our Review and are grateful for the opportunity to discuss the effects of exogenous testosterone on spermatogenesis and male fertility.

articles.title: Review of Management of Long-Term Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease
articles.abstract: To the Editor A recent Review provided a comprehensive discussion regarding long-term management of patients born with cyanotic congenital heart disease. As maternal-fetal medicine specialists, we would like to highlight the maternal and neonatal risks associated with both repaired and unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease in pregnancy and emphasize that all of these reproductive-aged patients should have pregnancy intentions routinely evaluated and be provided access to contraception, preconception, and multidisciplinary pregnancy care as appropriate.

articles.title: Review of Management of Long-Term Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease—In Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Dr Jones and colleagues for their thoughtful comments regarding our Review on survivors of cyanotic congenital heart disease and for highlighting the critical importance of reproductive health in women with congenital heart disease. We fully agree that reproductive counseling should be an integral component of lifelong care, particularly for women with complex congenital heart disease, and appreciate the opportunity to further emphasize this important aspect.

articles.title: Small Gains but Persistent Gaps in Statin Adherence
articles.abstract: Few problems in cardiovascular medicine have proved as resistant as adherence to effective medications. Nonadherence is pervasive and arises from the interplay of patient, treatment, clinician, payer, and health system factors. Decades of interventions to improve medication adherence have addressed forgetfulness, education, treatment complexity, and out-of-pocket costs, but have produced inconsistent or incremental gains, underscoring that nonadherence does not have a single remedy.

articles.title: Tenecteplase Before Thrombectomy at 4.5 to 24 Hours for Basilar Artery Occlusion Research Summary
articles.abstract: This trial evaluated whether tenecteplase before endovascular thrombectomy improved outcomes for patients with basilar artery occlusion treated 4.5 to 24 hours after estimated occlusion.

articles.title: Tenecteplase Before Thrombectomy for Basilar Artery Occlusion
articles.abstract: This randomized clinical trial evaluates the efficacy and safety of administering intravenous tenecteplase followed by endovascular thrombectomy vs endovascular thrombectomy alone in patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion.

articles.title: The Body and Poetry as Technologies
articles.abstract: If medicine too readily imagines the body as machine, the poem “Eternal life” proposes poetry itself as a deeper, more marvelously humane technology. Against a searchable database and a website’s archived obituary photographs, the poem offers its own elegant processing, synthesis, and preservation, which do not merely confirm whether someone has died, but restore the departed in the small gestures that make each one memorably human. Thus an implicit comparison emerges, with medicine’s view of decline and mortality as mechanical failure and retrievable data points contrasted with poetry’s returning of meaning, not a device for defeating or quantifying death, but a form for giving the deceased back to consciousness. The phone downloads a photograph and the website records a name as seamlessly as physicians might imagine how the brain stores and recalls memories. Yet neither can revivify the people the speaker’s father once knew, as it takes poetry to deliver the sweet sharing of sugar and the click of a returned key unlocking a door. The familiar medical fantasy of cybernetic immortality through synchronicity conquering biological decay is replaced by the strange kindness of poetry’s perfectly imperfect recollection, with loved ones absent at one moment but then lucidly present again the next. Forgetting, medically construed as neurological malfunction, becomes instead a porous border across which the dead may return through poetry’s dream-making. Poetry ultimately offers its own godlike machinery: “A last untouched memory/That kept giving them back to you/Eternally” concludes the poem, as if granting the eternal life announced in its title.

articles.title: The Pitfalls of Buying Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses the reasons behind the burgeoning black market for 2 unapproved GLP-1 weight loss drugs and the potential risks associated with their use.

articles.title: The Quiet Half of Good Medicine
articles.abstract: This Viewpoint discusses the need to discern when medical intervention is needed vs when supportive care and monitoring are appropriate.

articles.title: Treating In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Sodium Bicarbonate
articles.abstract: To the Editor The Bicarbonate for In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (BIHCA) trial demonstrated no significant improvement in return of spontaneous circulation with sodium bicarbonate administration, supporting current guidelines that do not recommend routine bicarbonate use during cardiac arrest. Nevertheless, several findings from the trial warrant further discussion.

articles.title: Treating In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Sodium Bicarbonate—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply In their letter about our recent BIHCA trial, Dr Gelbenegger and colleagues focus on the numerical differences in 30-day survival (12% vs 9.1%) and 30-day favorable neurological outcome (8.1% vs 5.4%) between groups. As noted, the trial was not powered for these outcomes and the results are uncertain. The 95% CIs for the risk ratio for 30-day survival ranged from 0.84 to 1.88 and for 30-day favorable neurological outcome from 0.82 to 2.34. As such, our results were compatible with harm, no effect, and benefit. Until well-conducted and sufficiently powered randomized clinical trials establish a benefit of sodium bicarbonate during cardiac arrest, consistent with international guidelines, we do not believe it should be administered routinely.

articles.title: Understanding Patent Thickets
articles.abstract: Prescription drug manufacturers typically apply to the US Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) for patents to protect their products from generic competition. The primary patent on a drug covers the core active ingredient and generally lasts 20 years. Because these patents are often granted early in drug development, however, the effective period of patent protection after US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval is usually 7 to 12 years. Once that period ends, generic versions may enter the market and compete with the brand-name drug, often leading to a rapid and substantial decline in price. The statutory framework for drug patents is established in the Hatch-Waxman Act of 1984. In addition to patent protection, brand-name drugs may qualify for periods of exclusivity granted by the FDA, which may run concurrently with patents or separately.

articles.title: Whole Grain Intake Tied to Lower Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors
articles.abstract: Consuming several servings of whole grains each day may lower certain risk factors for cardiovascular disease, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the European Heart Journal.

articles.title: High efficiency through light management in semitransparent perovskite-organic tandem modules for window-integrated photovoltaics
articles.abstract: This study combines voltage-matched perovskite and organic solar modules with a near-infrared distributed Bragg reflector to create semitransparent tandem photovoltaics for window integration. Independent submodule optimization and spectral light management deliver high efficiency while retaining visible transparency and color quality, and the concept is extended from 5 × 5 cm2 tandems to larger window demonstrators.

articles.title: Beyond thermoregulation: Active behavioural regulation of ultraviolet light exposure by a free‐ranging lizard
articles.abstract: This study provides a clear demonstration of active ultraviolet (UV) regulation in free‐ranging lizards and supports that microhabitat choice likely constrains UV regulation more than thermoregulation. Overall, it serves to establish UV as a parallel regulatory axis of physiological homeostasis and expand the range of testable hypotheses in animal ecology. Abstract Reptile behavioural ecology and regulatory behaviours have long been interpreted primarily through the lens of thermoregulation. However, basking and shuttling also expose animals to ultraviolet (UV) radiation necessary for vitamin D3 synthesis and other fitness‐relevant processes. Here, I adapt a standard thermoregulation framework to UV data to test whether lizards actively regulate UV exposure in nature. Using field observations, operative models, laboratory preference trials and custom‐built UV data loggers, I quantified the effectiveness of UV regulation and thermoregulation by ornate tree lizards (Urosaurus ornatus) across contrasting microhabitats (trees vs. snags). Lizards consistently preferred low UV exposures despite high environmental variation, particularly on snags. While U. ornatus thermoregulated equally well in both microhabitats, lizards were far more effective at UV regulation in trees than in snags. This difference likely reflects structural contrasts, as trees offer finer mosaics of sun and shade, whereas snags often impose unavoidable full‐sun exposure during basking. My results provide field evidence that wild lizards actively regulate their UV exposure. They further suggest that, for U. ornatus at least, the physiological consequences of microhabitat selection depend more strongly on UV conditions than on thermal conditions. Recognising UV regulation as a fundamental component of reptile homeostasis alongside thermoregulation, together with the trade‐offs between these regulatory demands, will broaden our understanding of reptile physiology and ecology and provide a stronger basis for predicting their ecological and evolutionary responses to environmental change.

articles.title: Contextually conspicuous species are more likely to be venomous: Habitat‐dependent aposematic colouration found throughout snakes
articles.abstract: Conspicuous colouration signals venomous nature throughout snakes. Abstract Many animals use conspicuous colours to advertise their unprofitability to potential predators, a phenomenon known as aposematism. For example, conspicuous banded patterns in snakes are often highlighted as aposematic signalling of their venomous nature. However, aposematic colouration needs to be analysed while considering a species' environmental context, seen as species which seem conspicuous in isolation may be well camouflaged within their natural environment. Here, we collate images for 458 snake species from iNaturalist and use a novel metric quantifying the degree of conspicuousness of each species compared with its natural context to test the relationship between conspicuousness and the presence, potency and defensive properties of venom. We find that venomous species are significantly more contextually conspicuous compared with non‐venomous species. However, while these results provide support for the link between the evolution of aposematism in relation to venom, we do not find an association with the potency or the pain‐inducing capacity of venoms with the data used in this study, indicating that these traits may not be important drivers of the evolution of aposematism in snakes. Our novel approach demonstrates how incorporating the environmental context of a species can shed light on our understanding of the evolution of conspicuous colouration.

articles.title: Contrasting associations between parental coordination and breeding success in albatrosses across differing environmental contexts
articles.abstract: Our study demonstrates that the benefits of parental coordination in albatrosses are context‐dependent rather than universal. Coordinated parental care enhanced reproductive success in stable environments, but had little effect in variable environments, where individual flexibility may be more valuable. These findings highlight how ecological unpredictability shapes the trade‐offs between joint investment and fitness. Abstract Understanding how animals acquire resources and allocate them to reproduction is fundamental for identifying the factors shaping fitness. In species with biparental care, both the amount each parent invests and how well their efforts are coordinated can influence reproductive success. Yet the benefits of coordination are unlikely to be universal and instead may depend strongly on species' ecology and environmental context. Despite this, many studies still focus on one parent in isolation, overlooking the potential importance of joint investment strategies. Here, we examined how parental effort and coordination, measured here as the relative investment of both parents, influenced breeding success in black‐browed Thalassarche melanophris and wandering albatrosses Diomedea exulans across colonies characterised by differing levels of environmental variability. We found that the influence of parental coordination on breeding success differed between species, breeding stages, and sites. Longer foraging trips improved annual breeding success during incubation for black‐browed albatrosses, whereas the effect of longer trips during brooding varied between sites subject to differing environmental variability. Similarity in the predictability and duration of partners' foraging trips was associated with higher breeding success at sites with higher environmental stability in both species but had little effect where conditions were more variable. This suggests that patterns of reproductive investment may differ according to environmental context, potentially reflecting a shift toward individual flexibility in more unpredictable conditions. Our findings underscore the importance of considering both parents' contributions when linking reproductive strategies to breeding outcomes and highlight how observed differences in breeding success across colonies may reflect shifts in the trade‐offs between self‐maintenance and offspring investment within varying environmental contexts.

articles.title: Direct, but not indirect, predation‐risk cues deter larval settlement in a scyphozoan jellyfish
articles.abstract: Predators can shape population dynamics before consumption occurs, with prey using chemical information to guide larval settlement. We show that jellyfish larvae (Aurelia coerulea) respond selectively to predation‐risk cues, reducing settlement in response to predator presence and active predation cues, but not to residual cues from previously preyed conspecific polyps. These findings highlight how non‐consumptive effects can influence recruitment in organisms with complex life cycles. Abstract Settlement represents a key transition from dispersal to recruitment, during which predation can strongly influence population dynamics through both consumptive and non‐consumptive effects. Predation generates chemical cues that convey information about the presence of predators, attacks on prey, ingestion of prey and post‐attack conditions. Predation‐risk cues can be direct, when emitted by the predator itself, or indirect, when released by prey, yet how larvae respond to these cues during settlement remains poorly understood in many systems. Here, we assessed how larvae of the scyphozoan jellyfish Aurelia coerulea respond to different predation‐risk cues by conducting four experiments manipulating predator kairomones, conspecific alarm cues, conspecific post‐attack cues and predator diet cues. We hypothesised that settlement responses would depend on the information provided by cues, with an avoidance response expected for those indicating direct predation risk. Settlement was deterred in response to direct cues (predator kairomones) and the combination of direct and indirect cues (predator kairomones with conspecific alarm cues). In contrast, settlement was unaffected by indirect cues alone (conspecific post‐attack cues) and cues not associated with predation (mechanical damage cues). In addition, predator diet cues had no further effect beyond that of predator kairomones alone. These results suggest that larval behaviour is shaped by predation risk, with information about the presence of predators playing a key role in eliciting antipredator responses during settlement. Our findings provide mechanistic evidence for understanding how predation‐risk cues mediate non‐consumptive effects during habitat selection in organisms with complex life cycles, highlighting how antipredator responses during a critical life‐history transition can influence recruitment success.

articles.title: Drought to deluge: Differential impacts of snow on mountain chickadee reproduction across the Sierra Nevada mountains
articles.abstract: Welklin et al. present a research framework that uses long‐term data to validate participatory science observations as measurements of reproductive success. Applying this framework to a long‐term study of mountain chickadees, they show that relationships between snow and chickadee reproduction vary across elevations and latitudes throughout the Sierra Nevada mountains. Abstract Changing climates are reshaping animal populations, but our understanding of how demographic trends are shaped by individual responses to local environmental conditions has historically been limited to long‐term studies with restricted spatial scales. Participatory science (i.e. citizen science) programs have improved our ability to identify geographic variation in population‐level trends, but these programs often lack insight into the individual‐level processes that underly such variation. Here we present a new research framework that uses long‐term data to validate participatory science observations as measurements of reproductive success, then explores reproductive responses to environmental variation across large geographic scales. We use this approach to investigate how reproduction in a montane songbird, the mountain chickadee (Poecile gambeli), varies in response to extreme scarcity and extreme accumulation of snow throughout the Sierra Nevada mountains in North America. Reproductive responses to snowfall extremes varied considerably across elevations and latitudes. In the northern Sierra Nevada, mountain chickadee reproductive performance was negatively affected by snow deluge conditions at high elevations, whereas snow drought conditions reduced reproductive output at low elevations. In the central Sierras, drought conditions negatively impacted both elevations, but deluge conditions improved reproductive performance at both low and high elevations. Reproduction in the southern Sierra Nevada was nearly unaffected by spring snow levels. These variable responses to extreme snow accumulation across environments corroborate increasing evidence that biological responses to environmental variation are often nonstationary across spatial scales. Our results show that long‐term studies can be used to inform and interpret participatory science data to provide a framework that strengthens our understanding of how individual behaviours underlie differential responses to environmental variation across geographic scales.

articles.title: Effects of heat stress on the foraging activity of incipient ant colonies
articles.abstract: Our work examines how thermal stress and exposure duration jointly influence the foraging dynamics of incipient Lasius niger colonies, a rarely studied stage in which limited workforce may heighten vulnerability. Abstract Global warming affects organismal performance across biological levels, from molecular processes to complex behaviours. Ectotherms are particularly vulnerable to thermal stress, as their body temperature critically depends on ambient environmental conditions. Warming may affect their foraging behaviour and/or their activity patterns. Here, we experimentally investigated the effects of acute and chronic thermal stresses on foraging by an ectotherm species. Social insects are important ecosystem engineers. Colony survival and growth depend on successful foraging, and colonies are more susceptible to warming when they are young and have fewer workers. We investigate how heat intensity and exposure duration influence foraging dynamics and survivorship in young colonies of the Lasius niger ant. Using laboratory assays, we studied the effects of acute heat stress by exposing foragers to short (10 min) and intermediate (1 h) heat pulses of 25°C (control), 30°C, 35°C and 40°C. Furthermore, we investigated the effects of chronic heat stress by rearing colonies at 25°C:20°C (day:night, control conditions) or 35°C:30°C (heat stress) for 2 weeks. After heat exposure, we recorded the latency to initiate foraging, the number of foraging visits and individual and colony survival between treatments. We hypothesized that ants could cope with relatively low and relatively short heat shocks, but not with high or long heat exposures. We found that prolonged and high heat exposure indeed increased the mortality of foragers and colonies, increased the delay before foraging, and decreased the number of foraging trips. Reduced foraging capacity in young colonies is likely to have strong fitness consequences. The establishment of colonies is dependent on the rapid acquisition of resources to sustain exponential growth. Any slowdown in resource intake can limit colony development and prolong the duration of the incipient (newly founded) and vulnerable stage, ultimately reducing the likelihood of successful establishment. Résumé Le réchauffement climatique affecte les performances des organismes à tous les niveaux d'organisation biologique, des processus moléculaires aux comportements complexes. Les ectothermes sont particulièrement vulnérables au stress thermique, car leur température corporelle dépend étroitement des conditions environnementales. L'augmentation des températures peut ainsi modifier leurs comportements de recherche de nourriture et leurs rythmes d'activité. Nous avons étudié expérimentalement les effets de stress thermiques aigus et chroniques sur le comportement de fourragement d'une espèce ectotherme. Les insectes sociaux ont un rôle majeur d'ingénieurs des écosystèmes. La survie et la croissance des colonies dépendent du succès du fourragement, et les jeunes colonies, qui ont un peu d'ouvrières, sont particulièrement sensibles au réchauffement climatique. Nous avons examiné comment l'intensité et la durée d'exposition à la chaleur influencent la dynamique du fourragement et la survie de jeunes colonies de la fourmi Lasius niger. À l'aide d'expériences en laboratoire, nous avons évalué les effets d'un stress thermique aigu en exposant des ouvrières fourrageuses à des épisodes de chaleur de courte durée (10 min) ou de durée intermédiaire (1 h) à 25°C (contrôle), 30°C, 35°C et 40°C. Nous avons également étudié les effets d'un stress thermique chronique en maintenant des colonies pendant deux semaines sous un régime thermique de 25°C:20°C (jour:nuit; condition contrôle) ou de 35°C:30°C (stress thermique). Après exposition à la chaleur, nous avons mesuré le délai avant l'initiation du fourragement, le nombre de sorties de fourragement, ainsi que la survie des individus et des colonies.…

articles.title: Evidence of parental care as a newly identified reproductive isolating barrier
articles.abstract: Behavioural variation can contribute to reproductive isolation and can be an important driver of speciation. Here, we show that a previously undescribed mechanism, parental care, can function as a postzygotic reproductive isolating barrier when dysregulated in hybrids. Abstract Variation in behaviour can contribute to reproductive isolation by preventing gene flow among populations. Here, we tested the novel hypothesis that parental care, when dysregulated, can function as a reproductive isolating mechanism in three‐spined stickleback fish (Gasterosteus aculeatus). In the typical ‘common’ stickleback ecotype, males provide care to their offspring by fanning with their pectoral fins and defending their nest. By contrast, a divergent ‘white’ stickleback ecotype has evolutionarily lost care and disperses embryos into the surrounding environment. We examined how paternal care from common, white and F1 hybrid fathers influenced offspring survival. We detected no intrinsic incompatibilities in embryos, but F1 hybrid fathers exhibited dysregulated parental care that coincided with decreased survival of parented offspring. The increased offspring mortality may be explained by further dysregulation of feeding and parenting circuitry, as F2 hybrids exhibited significantly higher rates of post‐fertilization filial cannibalism than common or white fathers. Additionally, despite strong divergence in nesting–building and courtship behaviour, F1 hybrids achieved mating success at a similar rate as male commons and whites, suggesting that prezygotic barriers against hybrids may be weak. The observed postzygotic isolation, and potentially weak prezygotic isolation in lab‐based studies, suggest that hybridization is likely occurring at low rates in the wild. Population genetic analysis supported this, as low proportions of putative hybrids were detected in sympatric sites. Together, these results may help explain why genetic divergence between these phenotypically distinct ecotypes is low and provide evidence that dysregulated parental behaviour can act as a newly discovered postzygotic reproductive isolating barrier.

articles.title: From thermoregulation to photoregulation: Ultraviolet radiation exposure is regulated by lizard behaviours
articles.abstract: Research Highlight: Lattanzio, M. S. (2026). Beyond thermoregulation: Active behavioural regulation of ultraviolet light exposure by a free‐ranging lizard. Journal of Animal Ecology, https://doi.org/10.1111/1365‐2656.70321. Exposure to ultraviolet radiation (UV) is both inevitable to any diurnal organism and a biological necessity for many animals. In many vertebrates, including lizards, UV exposure prompts important biological processes such as the endogenous production of vitamin D3. Overexposure, however, can damage DNA, cells and tissues. Despite an extensive literature on how heliothermic lizards regulate body temperatures in heterogeneous environments by moving between areas with different levels of sun exposure, very little attention has been given to how these organisms might also regulate UV exposure. In a study combining laboratory experiments to assess preferred body temperatures and levels of UV exposure and field observations of lizards in contrasting environments, Lattanzio (2026) demonstrates that ornate tree lizards (Urosaurus ornatus) are capable of effectively maintaining preferred body temperatures in environments with and without plentiful shade access. At the same time, lizards could effectively regulate their levels of UV exposure in environments with shade, but were poor at doing so on tree snags without sufficient cover. This suggests that lizards may suffer consequences, either due to the physiological impacts of overexposure to UV or due to behavioural trade‐offs, in these environments. Establishing the ecological relevance of UV exposure to lizard physiology, behaviours and life‐histories provides direction to exciting new research avenues, expanding the field of lizard thermoregulation to additional axes of environmental variation.

articles.title: Lockdowns as a natural experiment: Human presence, not buildings, drives mammal avoidance behaviour
articles.abstract: Graphical summary of the main findings in Potts et al. (2026). Using GPS‐collar data from 586 individuals spanning 23 mammal species (10 carnivores, 13 herbivores) across five continents, comprising over 1,100,000 location fixes, the study tested how COVID‐19 lockdown restrictions on human movement affected mammal avoidance behaviour. Overall, avoidance of human presence weakened by 36% during lockdown; carnivores showed roughly twice the reduction observed in herbivores, though this difference was not statistically confirmed. The relaxation in avoidance was context‐dependent on the Human Footprint Index (HFI): in high‐HFI landscapes (left), animals ranged measurably closer to infrastructure once human movement declined, while in low‐HFI landscapes (right), avoidance distances held steady. Together, these results indicate that ongoing human activity, rather than infrastructure itself, is the primary driver of mammal avoidance behaviour. Abstract Urban and rural infrastructures with their human inhabitants are usually difficult to distinguish as separate entities, as they almost always coexist. Consequently, it remains unclear whether wildlife avoids buildings due to the physical barriers themselves or because of the people who live and move around them. To address this question, the authors utilised GPS‐tracking data from 586 individuals of 23 terrestrial mammal species at 35 sites across the globe. The featured study treats the COVID‐19 lockdowns of 2020 as a natural experiment that temporarily restricted human movement without changing the built‐up environment. The authors show that avoidance of buildings weakened during lockdowns, but only in landscapes with a high Human Footprint Index; in more remote, natural areas, avoidance barely changed at all. This context‐dependent response suggests that it is the presence and movement of people, not infrastructure on its own, that shapes how mammals use human‐modified landscapes, a finding with direct relevance for forecasting wildlife responses to future changes in human activity.

articles.title: Paler within the city: Carotenoid‐based colouration covaries negatively with the proportion of impervious surface in great tit (Parus major) territories across Europe
articles.abstract: Across six European cities, great tits in more impervious territories had paler carotenoid‐based plumage, but not lower brightness or UV chroma. This suggests that urban habitat imperviousness is associated specifically with lower carotenoid pigment deposition, rather than broad changes in feather reflectance or structural quality. Abstract Urbanisation alters resource availability and exposes wildlife to novel environmental stressors, potentially driving phenotypic divergence. Carotenoid‐based plumage colouration is a condition‐dependent trait linked to dietary carotenoid acquisition and physiological allocation trade‐offs. Although urban populations are often reported to exhibit paler carotenoid colouration than rural populations, these patterns have rarely been tested along continuous fine‐scale urbanisation gradients at a continental scale. We investigated how reflectance parameters of the yellow breast plumage of adult Great Tit (Parus major) covary with territory‐scale local imperviousness, used here as a broad descriptor of urban habitat structure, across six European cities. Using 838 adult observations spanning 2005–2024 and sub‐meter‐resolution satellite imagery, we quantified the proportion of impervious surface within 100 m of nest boxes and related this metric to feather carotenoid chroma, brightness and UV chroma. Carotenoid chroma declined significantly with increasing impervious surface cover within breeding territories across Europe, corresponding to an expected decrease of 0.053 chroma units across the observed 0%–88% imperviousness gradient. This relationship remained robust across bootstrap resampling, leave‐one‐city‐out analyses and models controlling for among‐city variation in mean carotenoid chroma. Older individuals exhibited higher carotenoid chroma than yearlings, while males tended to be more chromatic and brighter than females. Impervious surface cover was not associated with feather brightness or UV chroma, indicating that urban habitat structure is linked specifically to carotenoid pigment deposition rather than feather structural properties and overall quality. Because carotenoid‐based colouration depends on dietary intake, higher levels of impervious cover and reduced vegetation may reflect lower availability of carotenoid‐rich resources in urban territories, although imperviousness should be interpreted as a multifactorial habitat descriptor rather than a direct mechanistic proxy. Our study provides the first continent‐scale evidence that carotenoid‐based colouration declines along a continuous urbanisation gradient. These findings identify plumage carotenoid chroma as a phenotypic correlate of local imperviousness within European cities and highlight the importance of fine‐scale habitat characterisation for understanding phenotypic responses to urbanisation. Future studies should test the mechanistic links between territory‐scale imperviousness, diet composition, pollutant exposure, physiological condition and fitness.

articles.title: Rapid loss, and slow recovery, of coral reef structural complexity resulting from a prolonged marine heatwave
articles.abstract: Using Structure‐from‐Motion photogrammetry in a longitudinal study, we show that although coral reef habitat complexity had declined significantly by the end of the most prolonged tropical marine heatwave on record, no further losses were detected and 3 years later the reef had begun to recover this critical ecosystem function. Abstract Globally, climate change‐driven marine heatwaves are causing increased coral bleaching and mortality events with cascading effects, including reef habitat complexity. Given that habitat complexity positively influences biodiversity and organismal abundance, such losses have negative ramifications for these ecosystems. Past studies have documented habitat complexity changes following heatwaves, yet the timing and persistence of habitat structural complexity losses arising from these events, and subsequent recovery rates, remain largely unknown. Here, we used Structure‐from‐Motion (SfM) photogrammetry to survey permanent shallow forereef quadrats (4 m × 4 m; n = 30) in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean at the epicentre of the third global coral bleaching event, the 2015–2016 El Niño, prior to, during and after the event. Reef three‐dimensional habitat complexity metrics calculated from the SfM images were then used to examine the immediate and long‐term impacts of the mass coral mortality. Coral reef structural habitat complexity, quantified as surface complexity (1.18‐fold decline), vector ruggedness measure (VRM; 1.52‐fold decline) and fractal dimension (1.03‐fold decline), declined significantly during the heatwave. However, contrary to expectation, no subsequent loss (i.e. due to erosion of dead coral colonies) was detected. We found that exposure to underlying local anthropogenic disturbance had already reduced reef complexity before the heatwave, such that the least disturbed sites showed the largest habitat complexity losses from it. All three complexity metrics increased significantly between 2017 and 2019, but not to pre‐heatwave levels. Furthermore, through fine‐scale morphological classification of the substrate, we show that all coral structure (regardless of whether dead or alive) contributed to habitat complexity, and that live submassive coral had the strongest correlation to the complexity metrics despite it seldom being mentioned in the literature as a morphology providing structural complexity. Morphologies contributing to habitat complexity also shifted over time, as more thermally sensitive corals (e.g. branching, foliose and tabulate) experienced much greater losses than thermally tolerant ones (e.g. submassive and massive). Our results illustrate how rapidly habitat complexity can be lost during climate change induced mass mortality events and imply complexity will be comprised of distinct coral morphologies on future coral reefs and that recovery will take many years.

articles.title: Sex differences in social dominance emerge late in life in a gregarious bird
articles.abstract: Male and female waxbills (Estrilda astrild) have similar social dominance as young adults but, in breeding seasons, most ageing females become subordinate. While sex differences in animals are often considered fixed, our findings reveal a plastic nature of sex differences, emerging when females face the challenges of old age and breeding. Abstract Social dominance shapes group structure and the collective behaviour of gregarious animals. Senescence, the progressive physiological deterioration associated with ageing, may influence behaviour, including social dominance, while reproductive roles may lead to different onset times or rates of senescence between the sexes. However, how ageing shapes sex differences in sociality remains poorly understood, largely due to the scarcity of long‐term studies comparing male and female social behaviour. To address this gap of knowledge, we monitored dominance hierarchies during foraging in an ageing, semi‐natural population of adult common waxbills (Estrilda astrild). Our study lasted 5 years, which is more than most adult waxbills would live in the wild, to facilitate detecting effects of senescence. At the onset of the study, sex differences in dominance were negligible but became pronounced with ageing during breeding seasons. In contrast, sex differences remained weak during non‐breeding seasons. Females showed stronger longitudinal and seasonal changes in dominance than males, whose dominance patterns remained more consistent across breeding and non‐breeding periods. Nonetheless, social dominance also increased, on average, as the number of years until death decreased. Although sex differences in animal sociality are often thought of as largely fixed, our findings reveal a dynamic pattern in which sex differences in dominance emerge with ageing and are context‐dependent, varying across breeding seasons. Overall, our results suggest that senescence and seasonal context shape sociality later in life.

articles.title: Sex‐specific responses to warming: A longitudinal study linking life‐history variation to telomere dynamics, telomerase expression and oxidative stress
articles.abstract: The study finds that climate warming reshapes sex‐specific life‐history trajectories without necessarily shortening telomeres, challenging the widely held assumption that thermal stress‐induced faster growth inevitably causes telomere erosion. It also demonstrates that time‐dependent telomerase maintains telomere length under warming conditions, particularly in fast‐growing males. Abstract Understanding how climate warming reshapes animal life histories is crucial for assessing population persistence and evolutionary trajectories. This is particularly important in ectotherms, whose physiology, performance and, ultimately, fitness are strongly influenced by environmental temperature. Because climate warming can alter key life‐history traits such as growth and survival, its effects may differ between sexes, potentially generating divergent organismal responses and long‐term consequences. Identifying the mechanisms underlying these sex‐specific patterns is therefore essential for explaining how ectotherms cope with warming environments. To determine whether climate warming induces sex‐specific life‐history responses and to elucidate physiological mechanisms underlying these responses, we conducted a longitudinal experiment in which toad‐headed agamas (Phrynocephalus przewalskii) were exposed to simulated higher temperatures under seminatural conditions. We specifically monitored growth, survival, telomere dynamics, telomerase expression and oxidative status throughout development. Males exposed to elevated temperatures showed accelerated growth and a slight reduction in survival, whereas females showed no detectable changes in growth or survival. This suggests divergent sex‐specific responses in life history to warming. At the physiological level, warming did not lead to telomere shortening; instead, the telomere length increased over time in both sexes. This was accompanied by a transient up‐regulation of telomerase expression in rapidly growing males, which could contribute to the maintenance of the telomere during accelerated growth. However, telomerase expression declined at the end of the experiment in both sexes exposed to warming. Finally, warming increased lipid oxidative damage in both sexes despite activation of antioxidant responses at elevated temperatures. Our results show that climate warming can reshape sex‐specific life‐history trajectories without necessarily inducing telomere shortening, challenging the expectation that faster growth under thermal stress is inevitably associated with telomere erosion. However, warming can still impose physiological costs with potential long‐term consequences for organismal health, as indicated by elevated oxidative damage. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating sex‐specific life‐history responses with physiological mechanisms to improve predictions of species responses to climate change.

articles.title: Weathering the storm: Most maternal and environmental drivers of individual reproductive success do not scale up to population recruitment in a large herbivore
articles.abstract: Using 18 years of data on eastern grey kangaroos, we show that drivers of individual reproductive success often do not scale up to population recruitment. Birth asynchrony could buffer population recruitment against environmental variability, such that variables affecting individual reproduction have little impact at the population level. Abstract Population growth depends upon individual survival and reproduction, but do drivers of individual reproductive success scale up to population recruitment? Factors affecting individuals may have little effect on population dynamics if individuals within a population experience different conditions. When seasonal resource availability is unpredictable and breeding season long, average conditions over a breeding cycle may poorly reflect the environment experienced by many individuals. We compared the drivers of individual reproductive success and population recruitment in an asynchronously breeding large herbivore, the eastern grey kangaroo (Macropus giganteus). We analysed 18 years of individual‐based data using multivariate hierarchical Bayesian models to first identify the causal mechanisms relating population density, environmental conditions and maternal traits to individual success. We then assessed whether the drivers of individual reproductive success scaled up to determine population recruitment. Most maternal and environmental covariates strongly influenced individual reproductive success, with distinct effects on juvenile survival before and after pouch exit. Maternal traits had a greater influence in the pouch, whereas environmental conditions became increasingly important once young exited the pouch. Most drivers of individual reproductive success did not affect population recruitment. Recruitment decreased with population density and increased with mean body condition of adult females. Weather harshness had a weak positive effect on recruitment, which appeared independent of female age structure, previous recruitment or forage. Most drivers of individual reproductive success did not scale up to population recruitment. Birth asynchrony could buffer population recruitment against environmental variation such that variables affecting individual reproduction have little impact at the population level. Large herbivores that reproduce asynchronously may therefore be more resilient to environmental variability than synchronous breeders.

articles.title: What does green mean? Modelling herbivore foodscapes and resource tracking in forested environments
articles.abstract: Preparing to sample fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium) in a recently burned forest patch in northern Idaho, USA. Abstract The forage maturation hypothesis predicts that herbivores should select plants at intermediate growth stages because they strike a balance between biomass and nutritional quality. Methods for identifying this key stage of plant phenology commonly rely on satellite-based greenness indices and their derivatives. By combining such indices with fine-scale movement data, ecologists have uncovered many novel behaviours and life-history strategies, including ‘green-wave surfing’ by herbivores. Yet, few studies have evaluated the degree to which greenness indices accurately reflect variation in forage characteristics or their selection by herbivores in forested habitats. We studied relationships among remotely sensed greenness indices, on-the-ground measures of forage biomass and quality and resource selection by white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), elk (Cervus canadensis) and moose (Alces alces) in the coniferous forests of northern Idaho, USA. We hypothesized that remote-sensing methods for measuring the green wave (i.e. the phenological progression of understory food plants) are not useful in coniferous forests because variation in greenness is driven mainly by conifers. We also hypothesized that patterns of forage selection by large herbivores are not detectable in the forest using greenness indices. We tested predictions derived from these hypotheses using on-the-ground measures of forage biomass and quality and more than 10 years of movement data from GPS collars. Remotely sensed greenness indices explained <2.5% of variation in forage biomass (adjusted R 2 < 0.024), which was more readily predicted by variation in tree canopy cover, topography and climate (total biomass: adjusted R 2 = 0.313; high-quality biomass: adjusted R 2 = 0.174). Moreover, with only one exception (elk selected pixels where the instantaneous rate of green-up was near its peak), greenness indices were among the least useful predictors of selection by large herbivores. Indeed, although all three species selected forage biomass, elk and moose simultaneously avoided greener pixels. Our results indicate that greenness indices are of limited value for predicting variation in forage resources or their selection by large herbivores in forested environments. Despite their intuitive appeal and ease of accessibility, such indices cannot always be substituted for on-the-ground measurements of plant traits that directly influence nutrient intake by herbivores.

articles.title: Plant diversity–mediated variation in root exudates regulates anaerobic nitrogen transformations in soil
articles.abstract: Among plant diversity metrics, phylogenetic diversity was the strongest predictor of root exudate chemodiversity. Root exudate carbon content promoted denitrification and DNRA, whereas greater chemodiversity was negatively associated with these pathways but positively associated with anammox. Carbohydrates and organic acids contributed more to explaining variation in N transformations than amino acids. These findings provide insights into the metabolite‐level mechanisms linking plant diversity to soil N transformations. Abstract Plants can regulate soil biogeochemical processes via root exudates, yet how exudate quantity and composition influence soil nitrogen (N) transformations remains unclear. We conducted complementary pot and microcosm experiments across gradients of plant species, phylogenetic and functional group diversity to examine effects of root exudates on anaerobic N transformation processes in soils, including dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), denitrification and anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox). Results showed that both rhizosphere metabolite and root exudate chemodiversity increased with multidimensional plant diversity, with phylogenetic diversity explaining more variance than species or functional group diversity. Carbohydrates and organic acids had stronger effects on N transformation processes than amino acids, with shikimic acid and sucrose identified as key components influencing DNRA and denitrification rates. Notably, higher exudate carbon (C) content significantly enhanced DNRA and denitrification, whereas exudate chemodiversity negatively correlated with these two processes but positively associated with anammox. Additionally, both exudate C content and chemodiversity directly or indirectly affected soil N transformations through changes in soil N availability, rather than microbial communities. Synthesis. These findings advance the mechanistic understanding of how plant diversity–mediated variation in root exudate quantity and composition regulates soil N cycling, highlighting its pivotal role in shaping ecosystem nutrient dynamics.
